name: What Families Should Know
title: What Families Should Know
answer: Families should know which tutoring tools their children use, how those tools are set up, and what support exists if they lack devices or internet. This matters because informed families can reinforce good tutoring habits at home, notice problems a teacher might miss, and actually use the school's equity plan when they know it exists.

sections.body: This idea is about giving families clear, practical information about the AI tutoring tools their children use. A short note can cover three things: the tool gives hints rather than answers, teachers can see conversation logs, and the school protects student information. The problem it solves is that families who do not understand a tool cannot support its use at home or spot issues a teacher might miss. It also addresses fairness, because families without devices or internet need to hear about the equity plan directly rather than having to ask. Clear information is presented as part of making personalized learning fair.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the practice starts with a short note home that explains how the tutoring tool behaves and how student information is handled. Parents can then help their children use tutors well by asking the child to explain what the tutor helped them understand, or to show how they solved a problem after getting a hint. If a child cannot explain the work, that is a signal the tutor may be doing too much, and this simple check at home reinforces the checks teachers do at school. For families without devices or internet, the school should tell them directly how to borrow a hotspot or when the library is open, because many families do not ask for help unless they know it is available. The text does not give separate grade band variations.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, drawing on the everyday experience that families who understand a tool can support its use at home and can spot problems a teacher might miss, and that families do not ask for help unless they know it is available.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks here are about information and fairness rather than technology. Families need to know which tools their children use and how those tools are set up, otherwise they cannot support use at home or catch problems. The check on whether a tutor is doing too much stays with the parent and child, since a child who cannot explain the work may be getting too much from the tool. The decision to share the equity plan directly, including how to borrow a hotspot or when the library is open, stays with the school. Nothing in the text removes teacher oversight, since teachers can see conversation logs and continue their own checks at school.
